teachbacks.text:
1. Customer presses Place order. The request carries customer id, cart id, a client-generated checkout token, and a payment method reference. Order (O1) receives it and generates an order id. Order has a unique constraint on the checkout token, so a double-click returns the existing order.
2. Order calls Cart over HTTP (K0) with the cart id. Cart replies with the current lines and prices, read only. If Cart fails, times out or is unreachable, Order replies HTTP 503. If the cart is missing or empty, it replies 422. In both cases (O1F) no order is stored, the token is not used up, the cart is untouched, and the customer can press Place order again.
3. Order (O2) saves the order in its own database with the cart lines and prices frozen, the cart id, and status PENDING_STOCK. From now on these frozen lines are the only source of truth.
4. Order calls Inventory over HTTP to reserve, passing the order id (I1). Inventory checks every line in one transaction. The call is idempotent on order id. If a reservation already exists it returns that state (RESERVED or CLAIMED gives "reserved"; EXPIRED or RELEASED gives "hold lapsed") instead of reserving again.
5. If any line is short, nothing is reserved. Inventory replies with the short items. Order (O3) sets REJECTED_SHORT_STOCK, stores the short items on the order, and replies with the order id and the list. The cart is unchanged.
6. If every line is in stock, Inventory (I2) does one local transaction. It reserves all lines, sets the reservation to RESERVED, and sets expires_at to 10 minutes ahead. It replies "reserved".
7. Order (O4) receives "reserved". It sets AWAITING_PAYMENT, writes a PaymentRequested event into its outbox table in the same local transaction, and replies HTTP 202 with the order id and "payment processing".
8. If Inventory does not answer within a few seconds or is unreachable, Order replies 202 with the order id and "checking stock". The order stays PENDING_STOCK. The Order sweeper is a loop inside Order. If an order has been PENDING_STOCK for over 1 minute, it resends the same reserve call. If the answer is "hold lapsed", Order (O3T) sets REJECTED_TIMEOUT, emails the customer to try again, and leaves the cart alone. No payment was requested, so there is nothing to refund. The customer needs a new Place order with a new token.
9. Meanwhile the screen polls Order by order id. Each status maps to a message: "checking stock", "payment processing", the short items, "could not hold your items in time", declined, confirmed, or "out of stock, refund on its way". Final results are also emailed, because the screen may be closed.
10. The outbox relay is a loop inside Order. About every second it reads the oldest outbox rows with empty published_at, publishes each to the broker, then sets published_at. A crash between those two steps causes a re-publish, so consumers must tolerate duplicates. No event is lost.
11. Payment consumes PaymentRequested. Each consumer does its local work, including the repeat check, in one transaction. It acknowledges the broker only after commit. On failure it does not acknowledge, and the broker redelivers.
12. Payment (P1) saves a payments row with status REQUESTED, unique per order id. The row holds amount, currency, the payment method reference, an attempt count, a next-attempt time and an acknowledged flag. The event carries everything Payment needs, so Payment never calls Order. Payment then sends an HTTPS charge to the provider. The order id is the idempotency key and also the reference field.
13. The HTTPS reply to the charge only means the provider accepted the request. Any final outcome in that reply is ignored. If the call fails or times out (P1a), a Payment loop retries rows that are still REQUESTED and unacknowledged. It retries with backoff and the same key, so there is no double charge. It stops at a retry limit.
14. The provider later sends a webhook, anywhere from seconds to 30 minutes after the charge. It may arrive more than once. P2 computes an HMAC of the raw body with a shared secret and compares it to the signature header. A bad signature gets HTTP 401 and nothing is read. P2 then reads the provider event id, the outcome, and the reference field (the order id).
15. If a valid webhook has no payment row, P2 does not record the event id, replies 503 so the provider redelivers, and alerts ops.
16. If the provider event id is already in processed_webhook_events, P3 ignores it and replies 200. Otherwise P4 runs one transaction. It inserts the event id and updates the payment status only if it is still REQUESTED. The unique key on the event id also catches duplicates.
17. If the outcome is declined, P5 sets DECLINED and publishes PaymentFailed. Order (O5) handles it only when AWAITING_PAYMENT. It sets PAYMENT_DECLINED, emails the customer, and publishes OrderFailed. Inventory (I4) then releases the hold if it is still RESERVED. It does this in a transaction that reads the status first. It subtracts `reserved`, sets RELEASED, and puts the stock back on sale. The cart is untouched.
18. If the outcome is succeeded, P6 sets SUCCEEDED and publishes PaymentSucceeded. Order (O6) acts on it when AWAITING_PAYMENT. It sets PAID_CLAIMING and calls Inventory over HTTP to claim stock for the order id.
19. Inventory claim. If the hold is RESERVED, one transaction subtracts `on_hand` and `reserved` per line and sets CLAIMED. If it is already CLAIMED, it replies "claimed" and changes nothing. If it is EXPIRED, it checks that every line has available (on_hand minus reserved) at least equal to the quantity. If so, it subtracts `on_hand` only and sets CLAIMED. If not, it changes nothing and replies "out of stock". If the hold is RELEASED or missing, it replies "out of stock".
20. Hold expiry. The expiry job (I3) is a loop in Inventory that runs about every 30 seconds. It finds RESERVED holds past expires_at and, in a transaction that checks the status is still RESERVED, subtracts `reserved` and sets EXPIRED. A hold can be returned up to one interval late. A claim arriving in that gap still succeeds. All of I3, I4 and claim serialise on the reservation row.
21. If the reply is "claimed", Order (O7) sets CONFIRMED, emails the customer, and publishes OrderConfirmed. The event carries the order id, cart id and ordered lines.
22. Cart (K1) consumes OrderConfirmed in one transaction. It inserts the order id into applied_orders (unique). If that collides, it is a repeat and nothing runs. Otherwise it subtracts the ordered quantities from the cart and deletes lines that reach zero. Changes the customer made after pressing Place order are kept.
23. If the reply is "out of stock", Order (O8) sets CANCELLED_OUT_OF_STOCK, emails the customer, and publishes RefundRequested. The cart is untouched.
24. Refund. Payment (R1) saves a refunds row PENDING for the full amount, unique per order id. R2 sends an HTTPS refund request to the provider with key = refund + order id. If the provider accepts, R3 sets REFUNDED and publishes RefundCompleted, and Order (O9) emails the customer that the refund is done. If the provider rejects, errors or times out, the row stays PENDING. The refund scheduler is a loop in Payment that runs about every minute. It retries PENDING or REFUND_FAILED rows whose next-attempt time has passed, with backoff and the same key. After N failures the row becomes REFUND_FAILED and ops is alerted, but retries continue and the row is never deleted before REFUNDED.
25. Stalled and contradictory cases. If an order is PAID_CLAIMING for over 1 minute (claim timed out, or Order crashed), the sweeper resends the same claim, which is safe to repeat. If an order is AWAITING_PAYMENT and no webhook arrives, Payment's reconciliation job handles it. For any payment still REQUESTED after about 35 minutes, it asks the provider about that key and goes through P4. If the provider has no record, Payment sets DECLINED and publishes PaymentFailed.
26. Status conflicts in Payment. P4 only changes REQUESTED payments. Success after DECLINED (P7) keeps DECLINED and publishes nothing to Order. It saves a refund row PENDING and alerts ops, and the normal refund path follows. Declined after SUCCEEDED does nothing except alert ops.
27. Status conflicts in Order. PaymentSucceeded arriving when Order is PAID_CLAIMING, CONFIRMED or CANCELLED_OUT_OF_STOCK is ignored. In any other non-AWAITING_PAYMENT status, Order leaves the status alone, publishes RefundRequested and alerts ops. PaymentFailed arriving when Order is PAYMENT_DECLINED is ignored. In any other non-AWAITING_PAYMENT status it is ignored with an ops alert.

teachbacks.text:
Walkthrough of one checkout, the happy path, with failure branches noted where the document gives them.

1. The customer presses Place order. The request carries customer id, cart id, a client-generated checkout token and a payment method reference. Order (O1) receives it and generates an order id. State: nothing is stored yet.

2. Order reads the cart over HTTP from Cart (K0), using the cart id. Cart only reads and returns current lines and prices. Failure: if Cart errors, times out or is unreachable, Order replies 503 "please try again". If the cart is missing or empty, it replies 422 "your cart is empty". In both cases (O1F) no order is stored, the token is not used up and the cart is untouched. The customer presses the button again.

3. Order stores the order (O2) in its own database. This writes the `orders` and `order_lines` rows with the lines and prices frozen and status `PENDING_STOCK`. The checkout token has a unique constraint. If the customer double-clicks, the second request collides on the token, reads the existing order and replies 202 with that order's current status text. From here on the frozen order is the source of truth, not the cart.

4. Order calls Inventory over HTTP to reserve stock, passing the order id (I1). In one local transaction Inventory checks every line.
   - If any line is short, nothing is reserved. The reply lists the short items. Order sets `REJECTED_SHORT_STOCK` and stores the short items on the order. The customer sees the list and the cart stays unchanged.
   - If all lines are in stock, Inventory (I2) writes the reservation in one transaction. Every line is reserved, the status is `RESERVED`, and it expires in 10 minutes. It replies "reserved".
   - Reserve is idempotent on order id. A repeat call returns the existing state: `RESERVED` or `CLAIMED` gives "reserved", and `EXPIRED` or `RELEASED` gives "hold lapsed". On "hold lapsed" Order sets `REJECTED_TIMEOUT` (O3T) and emails the customer to try again with a new checkout token.
   - If Inventory does not answer within a few seconds, or is unreachable, the customer gets 202 "checking stock". The order stays `PENDING_STOCK`. A sweeper loop inside Order resends the same reserve call for orders stuck over 1 minute, with no upper limit on retries.

5. On "reserved", Order (O4) sets `AWAITING_PAYMENT` and publishes `PaymentRequested`. It writes the status change and the event row to its `outbox` in one local transaction. Order then replies 202 "payment processing" with the order id. The event carries order id, customer id, total, currency and the payment method reference.

6. The outbox relay is a loop in Order. About every second it reads the oldest `outbox` rows with empty `published_at`, publishes each to the broker, then sets `published_at`. A crash between publishing and marking causes a re-publish, so consumers must tolerate duplicates. No event is lost.

7. The customer's screen keeps the order id and polls Order. The poll shows only the order's status text, per the status table. The customer is also emailed on each final result.

8. Payment consumes `PaymentRequested` (P1). Each consumer does its local work and its repeat check in one transaction, then acknowledges to the broker. If handling fails, nothing is acknowledged and the broker redelivers. P1 saves a `payments` row with status `REQUESTED` (unique per order id) before calling the provider. It then sends one HTTPS charge request with the amount, currency, payment method reference, the order id as idempotency key, and the order id as the reference field.

9. The charge reply only acknowledges acceptance. A success reply sets `provider acknowledged` = yes on the row. The final outcome in that reply is ignored.
   - If the call errors or times out, a payment loop retries rows that are `REQUESTED` with acknowledged = no. It uses backoff and the same key, so there is no double charge. The row keeps an attempt count and next attempt time.
   - At the retry limit the retries stop. The row stays `REQUESTED` until the reconciliation job (35 minutes) asks the provider about that idempotency key. If the provider has no record, Payment sets `DECLINED` and publishes `PaymentFailed`. If it has a record, Payment follows the recorded outcome through P4.

10. The provider later sends a webhook (seconds to about 30 minutes, possibly more than once). P2 computes an HMAC of the raw body with a shared secret and compares it with the signature header. A bad signature gets 401 and nothing is read. Otherwise P2 reads the provider event id, the outcome and the reference (the order id), and finds the payment by order id. If no payment row exists, P2 does not record the event id, replies 503 so the provider redelivers, and alerts ops. If the event id was already processed, P3 ignores it and replies 200.

11. P4 runs in one transaction. It inserts the event id into `processed_webhook_events` (unique) and updates the payment status only if it is still `REQUESTED`. The webhook and the reconciliation job both go through P4, and whichever commits first wins.
    - Succeeded: P6 sets `SUCCEEDED` and publishes `PaymentSucceeded`, again via the outbox.
    - Declined: P5 sets `DECLINED` and publishes `PaymentFailed`. Order (O5) then marks `PAYMENT_DECLINED`, emails the customer and publishes `OrderFailed`. Inventory (I4) releases the hold only if it is still `RESERVED`, setting `RELEASED` and putting the stock back on sale. The cart is untouched.
    - If the payment is already final when a different outcome arrives, the status table says what to do. Success after `DECLINED` (P7) keeps `DECLINED`, saves a refund row `PENDING` and alerts ops. Declined after `SUCCEEDED` does nothing except alert ops. A repeat of the same outcome does nothing except save the event id.

12. Order consumes `PaymentSucceeded` (O6) and decides by its current status.
    - `AWAITING_PAYMENT`: the normal path. Order sets `PAID_CLAIMING` and calls Inventory over HTTP to claim, passing the order id.
    - `PAID_CLAIMING`, `CONFIRMED` or `CANCELLED_OUT_OF_STOCK`: a repeat event, so it is ignored.
    - Any other status: Order leaves the status alone, publishes `RefundRequested` and alerts ops. The customer gets only the later `RefundCompleted` email.

13. Inventory handles the claim in one transaction, following its claim table.
    - `RESERVED`: for each line, `on_hand` and `reserved` are both reduced by the quantity. Status becomes `CLAIMED`. Reply "claimed".
    - `CLAIMED` (a repeat): do nothing and reply "claimed".
    - `EXPIRED`: if every line has available (`on_hand` minus `reserved`) at least the quantity, reduce `on_hand` only and set `CLAIMED`. Otherwise change nothing and reply "out of stock".
    - `RELEASED` or no reservation: reply "out of stock".
    - The 10-minute expiry (I3) is a loop in Inventory that runs about every 30 seconds. It expires `RESERVED` holds past `expires_at`. Like I4, it writes only if the status is still `RESERVED`. Everything serialises on the reservation row, so `reserved` is never subtracted twice.

14. "Claimed" (O7): Order sets `CONFIRMED`, emails the confirmation and publishes `OrderConfirmed` (order id, cart id, ordered lines). The email is sent after the commit and is best-effort. A failure is logged and alerted, and the status is not rolled back.

15. Cart consumes `OrderConfirmed` (K1). In one transaction it inserts the order id into `applied_orders` (unique). If the insert collides, the event is a repeat and nothing runs. Otherwise it subtracts the ordered quantities from the cart and deletes lines that reach zero. Anything the customer added after pressing Place order is kept. The poll now shows "Order confirmed".

16. The "out of stock" branch (O8) is taken when the claim reply is "out of stock", for example after a late success. Order sets `CANCELLED_OUT_OF_STOCK`, emails the customer and publishes `RefundRequested`. Payment (R1) saves a refund row `PENDING` for the full amount (unique per order id) before calling the provider. R2 sends an HTTPS refund request with the key "refund + order id".
    - Accepted: R3 sets `REFUNDED` and publishes `RefundCompleted`. Order (O9) emails the customer that the refund is done.
    - Rejected, error or no answer: the row stays `PENDING`. A refund scheduler loop in Payment runs about every minute. It retries `PENDING` and `REFUND_FAILED` rows whose next attempt time has passed, with backoff and the same key. After N failures the row becomes `REFUND_FAILED` and ops is alerted, but retries continue and the row is never deleted until `REFUNDED`.

17. Crash recovery in Order. If an order sits in `PAID_CLAIMING` for over 1 minute, the sweeper resends the same claim. Claim is safe to repeat, so the answer is the same. An order in `PENDING_STOCK` or `PAID_CLAIMING` for over 10 minutes alerts ops once. If Inventory stays down, retries are unlimited. For `AWAITING_PAYMENT` with no webhook, recovery is Payment's reconciliation job.

Walkthrough: one order, happy path first, then branches.

1. Trigger. The customer presses Place order. The request carries customer id, cart id, a client-generated checkout token (a UUID made once per attempt and resent unchanged on a repeat press), and a payment method reference. Order (O1) generates an order id.

2. Cart read. Order makes an HTTP call to Cart (K0) with the cart id. Cart is read-only here and returns current lines and prices. If Cart errors, times out or is unreachable, Order replies 503 "please try again". If the cart is missing or empty, it replies 422 "your cart is empty". In both cases (O1F) no order is stored, the token is not used up, and the cart is untouched.

3. Store the order. Order (O2) saves the order with the cart lines and prices frozen, status PENDING_STOCK, the cart id and the token. The token has a unique constraint. If a double-click repeat hits that constraint, Order reads the existing order and replies 202 with its order id and the text for its current status. From here the frozen lines and prices are the only source of truth.

4. Reserve stock. Order calls Inventory over HTTP with the order id (I1). Inventory checks every line in one transaction.
   - If any line is short, nothing is reserved. The reply lists the short items. Order (O3) sets REJECTED_SHORT_STOCK, stores the short items, and emails the customer. The cart is unchanged.
   - If all lines are in stock, Inventory (I2) does one local transaction. It reserves all lines (increasing `reserved` on the stock rows), creates a reservation row RESERVED with expires_at 10 minutes out, and replies reserved.
   - Reserve is idempotent on order id. An existing RESERVED or CLAIMED reservation returns "reserved". An EXPIRED or RELEASED one returns "hold lapsed". With no reservation, I1 and I2 run.
   - If Inventory does not answer within a few seconds, Order replies 202 "checking stock" and leaves the order PENDING_STOCK. The sweeper retries (step 12).

5. Order handles the reserve reply. It applies the change only if the order is still PENDING_STOCK, so a duplicate reply is applied once. For "reserved" (O4), it sets AWAITING_PAYMENT and writes PaymentRequested to its outbox in the same local transaction, then replies 202 "payment processing" if the call came from Place order. For "hold lapsed" (O3T), it sets REJECTED_TIMEOUT and emails the customer to retry with a new token. No payment was requested, so there is nothing to refund.

6. Outbox relay. A loop inside Order wakes about every second. It reads the oldest outbox rows with empty published_at, publishes each to the broker, then sets published_at. A crash between publishing and marking causes a re-publish, so every consumer must tolerate duplicates. Events are never lost. Consumers do all their local work and their repeat check in one transaction, then acknowledge to the broker. If handling fails, nothing is acknowledged and the broker redelivers.

7. Customer screen. It keeps the order id and polls Order by order id. The poll shows only the order status: PENDING_STOCK shows "checking stock", AWAITING_PAYMENT and PAID_CLAIMING show "payment processing", and so on per the table. Emails go out for final results. They are sent after the status commits and are best-effort. A failed email is logged and ops is alerted, and the status is not rolled back.

8. Charge. Payment consumes PaymentRequested (order id, customer id, amount, currency, payment method reference). P1 saves a payments row (REQUESTED, unique per order id) before calling the provider. It then sends an HTTPS charge request with the order id as both idempotency key and reference. A success reply only means "accepted", and Payment sets `provider acknowledged` = yes. Any outcome in that reply is ignored. If the call errors or times out, Payment retries with the same key and backoff, so there is no double charge. A payment loop retries rows that are REQUESTED with acknowledged = no. It stops at a retry limit, and the row stays REQUESTED.

9. Webhook. The provider later sends a webhook, from seconds to about 30 minutes, possibly more than once. P2 computes an HMAC of the raw body with a shared secret and compares it with the signature header. A bad signature gets 401 and nothing is read. The body carries the provider event id, the outcome and the reference (the order id), and Payment finds the payment by that order id. If no payment row exists, it does not record the event id, replies 503 so the provider redelivers, and alerts ops.
   - If the event id is already in processed_webhook_events, P3 ignores it and replies 200.
   - Otherwise P4 runs one transaction. It saves the event id and updates the payment status only if it is still REQUESTED.
   - Declined (P5): status DECLINED, publish PaymentFailed.
   - Succeeded (P6): status SUCCEEDED, publish PaymentSucceeded. Both go through Payment's outbox. The document says Order and Payment have outboxes, and that Payment publishes these events.

10. Success path. Order receives PaymentSucceeded. If the order is AWAITING_PAYMENT (O6), it sets PAID_CLAIMING and calls Inventory over HTTP to claim. Inventory's claim rules:
   - Hold RESERVED: `on_hand` and `reserved` are decreased per line, status becomes CLAIMED, reply claimed.
   - Hold CLAIMED (a repeat): reply claimed.
   - Hold EXPIRED: if every line has available >= qty, `on_hand` is decreased and the status becomes CLAIMED (reply claimed). Otherwise nothing changes and the reply is out of stock.
   - Hold RELEASED, or no reservation: reply out of stock.
   On "claimed", Order (O7) sets CONFIRMED, emails the customer, and publishes OrderConfirmed (order id, cart id, lines). Cart (K1) consumes it in one transaction. It inserts the order id into applied_orders (unique), subtracts the ordered quantities, and deletes lines that reach zero. If the insert collides, it is a repeat and nothing happens. Anything the customer added to the cart after pressing the button is kept.
   - If PaymentSucceeded arrives when the order is PAID_CLAIMING, CONFIRMED or CANCELLED_OUT_OF_STOCK, Order ignores it as a repeat.
   - For any other status, Order leaves the status alone, publishes RefundRequested and alerts ops.

11. Failure branches after payment.
   - Declined. Order receives PaymentFailed while AWAITING_PAYMENT (O5), sets PAYMENT_DECLINED, emails the customer, and publishes OrderFailed. Inventory (I4) releases the hold only if it is still RESERVED. The cart is untouched. A repeat PaymentFailed in PAYMENT_DECLINED is ignored. In any other status, Order ignores it and alerts ops.
   - Out of stock after payment (late success). The 10-minute hold may have been returned by the expiry job (I3). I3 runs about every 30 seconds, selects RESERVED holds past expires_at, sets EXPIRED, and decreases `reserved`. When the claim finds no stock, Order (O8) sets CANCELLED_OUT_OF_STOCK, emails the customer, and publishes RefundRequested. Payment (R1) saves a refund row PENDING for the full amount (unique per order id), then (R2) requests the refund from the provider with the key refund + order id. If the provider accepts, the row becomes REFUNDED and Payment publishes RefundCompleted. Order (O9) emails the customer that the refund is done. If the provider rejects or gives no answer, the row stays PENDING. The refund scheduler runs about every minute and retries rows that are PENDING or REFUND_FAILED and due, with the same key and backoff. After N failures the row becomes REFUND_FAILED and ops is alerted, but retries continue and the row is never deleted until REFUNDED.
   - Success after DECLINED (P7). Status stays DECLINED and nothing is published to Order. Payment saves a refund row PENDING, alerts ops, and follows the normal refund path.
   - Other conflicting outcomes. Success then declined: nothing changes and ops is alerted. The same outcome again: nothing happens, though the event id is saved.

12. Recovery loops in Order.
   - An order in PENDING_STOCK for over 1 minute (crash, lost reply, Inventory unreachable): the sweeper repeats the same reserve call and handles the reply as in step 5.
   - An order in PAID_CLAIMING for over 1 minute: the sweeper repeats the claim.
   - AWAITING_PAYMENT with no webhook: Payment's reconciliation job. For payments still REQUESTED after about 35 minutes, it asks the provider for the status by idempotency key. If the provider has no record, Payment sets DECLINED and publishes PaymentFailed. If it has a record, Payment follows the recorded outcome. Both go through P4's conditional update, so whichever of the webhook and the job commits first wins.
   - The sweeper retries with no upper limit. Ops is alerted once if an order is stuck in PENDING_STOCK or PAID_CLAIMING for over 10 minutes.

13. Multiple instances. All loop steps are safe to repeat, so two instances picking up the same row only waste work.

How often the screen polls, and the poll response shape, are not given.

The broker product, whether consumers are pushed or pull events, how many redeliveries happen before an event goes to the dead-letter queue, and where parked events go are not known. The document says only that a parked event must alert ops.
How the ops alerting channel and the email sender are reached (interface, protocol) is not specified.
How the customer obtains the payment method reference (for example a provider-hosted form) is not stated.
The payment provider is not named. The webhook format, signature header name, HMAC details, status lookup by idempotency key, and refund API are assumptions, so I do not know the real provider calls.

The document does not say what Order replies, beyond the order id and short items, when Inventory returns short stock to Place order, such as the HTTP status code. It calls this the fourth reply, not a 202.

All timing and limit values are placeholders and undecided: the few-second waits for Cart and Inventory, the charge and refund retry limits and backoff, the refund failure count N, the refund scheduler interval, and the 10-minute ops alert threshold.
Whether the provider can report a refund as failed by webhook after accepting it is unknown.
Whether rows are locked when several instances of a service run the loops is undecided.
What happens when a long Inventory outage leaves orders in PAID_CLAIMING beyond the single ops alert (for example refunding them) is undecided.
The document does not say how the reconciliation job's 35 minutes relates to when it runs (its interval), or how Order sweeper stalled-state ages are measured.
The document does not say what the poll shows for REJECTED_SHORT_STOCK beyond the short items, or how the customer's email wording is chosen.

Cart and Inventory do not publish events, so they have no outbox. The document does not say how Inventory consumes OrderFailed more precisely than the I4 release rule, nor how event delivery to Cart is retried beyond broker redelivery.
